about: Words of the Constitution the Supreme Court has declared invalid or void, checked against each judgment (S.C.R. pages in at). Supreme Court only. Shown as a box and clause labels on article and Schedule pages; the official text itself is unchanged. Rebuilt from a check of all 106 amendments on 24 November 2026.

items.say: The words "and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy" were struck down in Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973). They are still printed in the official text, but they have no effect.

The 1976 change to "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" was declared void in Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980). In 2024 a nine-judge bench held that the article as it stood before 1976 (covering clauses (b) and (c) of article 39) remains in force, to the extent Kesavananda Bharati upheld it.

Clauses (4) and (5), added in 1976, were declared void in Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980): they barred courts from reviewing amendments and removed every limit on the amending power. They are still printed in the official text, but they have no effect.

Clause (5) and its proviso were declared unconstitutional and void in P. Sambamurthy v State of Andhra Pradesh (1986). They made the Administrative Tribunal's final orders take effect when the State Government confirmed them or after three months, whichever came first, and let the State Government change or cancel them. They are still printed in the official text, but they have no effect.

say.a:323A: Sub-clause (d) of clause (2) lets a law shut out every court except the Supreme Court under article 136. In L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India (1997) the Supreme Court held it unconstitutional to the extent it shuts out the High Courts under articles 226 and 227 and the Supreme Court under article 32.
say.a:323B: Sub-clause (d) of clause (3) lets a law shut out every court except the Supreme Court under article 136. In L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India (1997) the Supreme Court held it unconstitutional to the extent it shuts out the High Courts under articles 226 and 227 and the Supreme Court under article 32.

items.say: This article was put in by the Ninety-ninth Amendment (2014), which set up the National Judicial Appointments Commission. The Supreme Court declared the whole amendment unconstitutional and void in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India (2015), and held that the way Judges were appointed and transferred before it applies. It is still printed in the official text, but it has no effect.

items.say: Clause (4), put in by the Thirty-ninth Amendment (1975), placed the elections of the Prime Minister and the Speaker beyond the election law and any challenge. The Supreme Court struck it down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975), and one judge, Chandrachud J, also held clause (5) void. The whole article was omitted in 1979.

Paragraph 7, which barred every court from questions of disqualification under this Schedule, was declared invalid in Kihoto Hollohan v Zachillhu (1992), because it was not ratified by half the States as article 368(2) requires. The rest of the Schedule was upheld. Paragraph 7 is still printed in the official text, but it has no effect.

The Ninety-seventh Amendment (2011), which added this Part, needed ratification by half the State Legislatures under article 368(2) and did not get it. In Union of India v Rajendra N. Shah (2021) the Supreme Court held that the Part therefore applies only to multi-State co-operative societies, in the States and in the Union territories. For other co-operative societies it has no effect.
